title: Wucherpfennig v. Dooley
summary: A response that announces readiness to proceed and financing arranged but asks the offeror what exact amount she expects, and whether she will sign a special-use-valuation agreement, is not the absolute and unequivocal acceptance North Dakota requires; it continued negotiations, so the offeror was free to revoke.
notes: Court: Supreme Court of North Dakota (1984).

sections.Parties: Donald Wucherpfennig, the plaintiff and appellant, sought specific performance of an alleged contract to buy his sister’s interest in inherited farmland. Elizabeth Dooley, his sister, was the defendant and appellee. Their sister Louise Grettum and others claiming interests in the land were also named, though the disputed sale concerned only Elizabeth’s share. Justice Sand wrote for the Supreme Court of North Dakota on July 11, 1984.
sections.Material Facts: The siblings inherited a farm of four quarters after their father died in 1964 and their mother in 1977: Donald held an undivided two-thirds of the farmstead quarter and each sister one-sixth, and each held one-third of the other three quarters. During probate Elizabeth wrote on January 4, 1979 to Robert Case, the estate’s attorney, offering to sell her share to Donald at $200 an acre for cash, handled promptly; no one disputed that this was an offer. Case replied on January 13 that Donald was interested. On February 17 Case wrote that Donald had arranged Federal Land Bank financing and was ready to proceed, then asked Elizabeth to state the exact amount she expected for her interest and whether she would sign a Special Use Valuation agreement, requesting a response on both. She did not answer, and on March 9 she revoked the offer.
sections.Procedural History: Donald sued for specific performance of the alleged sale and, alternatively, for partition. By consent the specific-performance claim was tried first. The district court found that Donald had not accepted Elizabeth’s offer and that even if he had, the supposed contract could not be specifically enforced, giving four independently sufficient grounds for dismissal. On appeal Donald had to defeat every ground. The Supreme Court of North Dakota agreed that there was no acceptance, expressly declined to decide the other issues, and affirmed the dismissal; the partition claim was not resolved in the reported decision.
sections.Issue: Did the February 17 letter, stating that Donald had arranged financing and was ready to proceed while asking Elizabeth for the exact amount she expected and about a special-use-valuation agreement, communicate an unconditional acceptance that formed a contract before she revoked on March 9?
sections.Holding: No. Under N.D. Century Code § 9-03-21 and the governing precedents, an acceptance must be absolute, unequivocal and unconditional, must concern the same bargain as the offer, and must express an intention to create the contract through that response itself. Read as a whole, the letter showed preparation and continued interest but left a material aspect of the exchange open and contemplated further negotiation; Donald had not unequivocally committed himself to the transaction Elizabeth described. The dismissal of the specific-performance claim was affirmed on that ground alone.
sections.Reasoning: The court read the letter as a whole. Arranging financing showed Donald was preparing to buy and readiness to proceed showed continuing interest, but the immediate request for the amount Elizabeth expected indicated that a material part of the exchange remained open, so the letter was movement toward a future agreement rather than assent that itself completed the bargain. Donald’s own testimony reinforced the reading: asked why the letter named no total, he said the amount would have been $37,200, acknowledged that Elizabeth would have expected more, and admitted she would not have signed a contract stating his figure. The parties therefore had not assented to the same terms. Under Restatement §§ 59 and 61 a reply conditioning assent on different terms is a counteroffer, while a completed acceptance may carry a nonconditional request; here the threshold commitment was missing, so the court did not need to classify the letter as a counteroffer. Donald’s financing arrangements showed preparation, not acceptance of a cash-sale offer, and reliance was not treated as a formation argument.

The following Hill’s v. Kessler problem asks whether an order acknowledgment promising attention communicates more than interest or preparation.

sections.Parties: Donald Wucherpfennig sought specific performance against his sister Elizabeth Dooley regarding her inherited interest in family farmland.
sections.Material Facts: Dooley offered by letter to sell for $200 per acre in a cash transaction handled promptly. An attorney first said Donald was interested, then wrote that financing was arranged and he was ready to proceed, asking for the exact dollar amount she expected and whether she would sign a tax-related agreement. She later revoked. Donald testified that his intended $37,200 price was below what he believed she expected and that she would not have signed a contract at that amount.
sections.Procedural History: The district court dismissed the claim for specific performance on four alternative grounds. The North Dakota Supreme Court affirmed on the ground that no acceptance occurred and expressly did not reach the remaining grounds.
sections.Issue: Did the February letter form a contract before the seller’s revocation?
sections.Holding: No. It did not express an absolute, unequivocal, unconditional intent to create a contract without further agreement.
sections.Reasoning: The wording and the surrounding evidence described ongoing negotiations, not a present commitment to the same bargain. Financing arrangements were preparatory. The request for the expected total and Donald’s testimony reinforced the conclusion that agreement had not yet been reached. The fact that the court could affirm on one independent ground limits what the decision establishes about the others.

learning.why: The case asks whether the offeree has actually exercised the power of acceptance. Preparations and a favorable reaction are evidence to interpret, not automatic acceptance.

topics.acceptance: The response did not communicate present and unconditional agreement.
topics.assent: The parties’ communications and known disagreement over price mattered.
topics.definiteness: An unresolved total reinforced the conclusion that negotiation continued.
topics.offer: An offer can remain unaccepted despite preparation to perform.
